scenes.visual: Title card 'What the Island's Counts Show' over a flat cartoon of a small plane flying above a snowy island. COLOUR MAP (same as the first film): moose BROWN, wolves GREY, plant food GREEN; counter box top right in every scene after the title, white text on charcoal: 'moose per wolf: N'. The graph in this film is computed from the National Park Service winter counts for 1980 to 2026 (label 'NPS winter counts'); cartoons are labelled 'schematic'. All numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Does the real island follow the rule? The first film used a model island, where wolves usually ran short of food before the moose ran out. Now we check the real counts.
scenes.visual: The question appears as on-screen text. A quick replay of the first film's model island with its loop arrow and the counter dropping to orange, labelled 'model (schematic)'. Then it slides away to reveal a map of Lake Superior with Isle Royale highlighted.
scenes.narration: Does the real island follow the rule? The first film used a model island, where wolves usually ran short of food before the moose ran out. Now we check the real counts.

scenes.tts: Isle Royale is an island in Lake Superior, where wolves hunt moose. Scientists survey both animals in most winters. Wolves are counted from the air, so the wolf count is close to every wolf.
scenes.visual: Cartoon plane (schematic) flies over the snowy island. Below, grey wolf tracks and a grey pack stand out against white snow; tally marks appear in a box labelled 'wolves: counted from the air'.
scenes.narration: Isle Royale is an island in Lake Superior, where wolves hunt moose. Scientists survey both animals in most winters. Wolves are counted from the air, so the wolf count is close to every wolf.

scenes.tts: Moose are too many to count one by one. Scientists count them on small squares of land and use those counts to estimate the whole island. So moose numbers are estimates.
scenes.visual: A grid of small squares is laid over the island map; a few squares light up and show brown moose icons being counted. An arrow from the lit squares to a big label 'moose: estimated for the whole island'.
scenes.narration: Moose are too many to count one by one. Scientists count them on small squares of land and use those counts to estimate the whole island. So moose numbers are estimates.

scenes.tts: Here are the counts from many winters. The brown line is the moose. The grey line is the wolves. Some winters have no count.
scenes.visual: A two-panel line graph draws itself left to right over 1980 to 2026: top panel brown line 'moose (estimated)' on a scale 0 to 2,500; bottom panel grey dashed line 'wolves (counted)' on a scale 0 to 50, sharing one year axis. Dotted gaps at 2021 and 2025 labelled 'no count'. Source label: 'NPS winter counts'.
scenes.narration: Here are the counts from many winters. The brown line is the moose. The grey line is the wolves. Some winters have no count.

scenes.tts: Look at nineteen ninety-five. The moose line is near its highest point. There are only sixteen wolves. The counter is high, so the wolves had plenty of moose to hunt.
scenes.visual: A vertical highlight bar drops on 1995 across both panels. On-screen labels: '1995: about 2,400 moose', '16 wolves'. Counter: 'moose per wolf: 150'.
scenes.narration: Look at nineteen ninety-five. The moose line is near its highest point. There are only sixteen wolves. The counter is high, so the wolves had plenty of moose to hunt.

scenes.tts: Two winters later, the moose had dropped to about five hundred. The wolves had risen to twenty-four. The counter fell, and the wolves now had few moose to hunt.
scenes.visual: The highlight bar slides to 1997. Labels: '1997: about 500 moose', '24 wolves'. Counter rolls down from 150 to 'moose per wolf: 21' and turns orange.
scenes.narration: Two winters later, the moose had dropped to about five hundred. The wolves had risen to twenty-four. The counter fell, and the wolves now had few moose to hunt.

scenes.tts: The counts alone do not say why the moose fell. Weather and food can matter too. What we can follow is the counter.
scenes.visual: A small card over the 1995 to 1997 drop in the brown line: 'why did moose fall? counts alone do not say'. Small icons for weather (snowflake) and food (green tree) appear beside it with a question mark.
scenes.narration: The counts alone do not say why the moose fell. Weather and food can matter too. What we can follow is the counter.

scenes.tts: So here is a question for you. Only about twenty-one moose for each wolf. What happens to the twenty-four wolves by the next winter? Pause and predict.
scenes.visual: Question card: 'Only 21 moose for each wolf. What happens to the 24 wolves by next winter?' The grey wolf line in the bottom panel stops at 1997; the counter pulses orange.
scenes.narration: So here is a question for you. Only about twenty-one moose for each wolf. What happens to the twenty-four wolves by the next winter? Pause and predict.

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds; a 5-second ring timer fills at bottom right.

scenes.tts: By the next winter, there were only fourteen wolves. Hundreds of moose were still alive. That fits the rule from the first film.
scenes.visual: The grey line draws on to 1998 and drops: label '1998: 14 wolves'. In the top panel the brown line shows '1998: about 700 moose', with a ring labelled 'hundreds of moose still alive'. A tick mark: 'fits the rule'.
scenes.narration: By the next winter, there were only fourteen wolves. Hundreds of moose were still alive. That fits the rule from the first film.

scenes.tts: But be careful. One run of counts can fit the rule. It cannot prove the cause by itself.
scenes.visual: Two labelled boxes side by side: 'fits the rule' (ticked) and 'proves the cause' (crossed out, with a small note 'other things changed too').
scenes.narration: But be careful. One run of counts can fit the rule. It cannot prove the cause by itself.

scenes.tts: Now jump to twenty sixteen. Scientists counted only two wolves on the whole island. They estimated one thousand three hundred moose. The counter shoots way up.
scenes.visual: The highlight bar jumps to 2016. Labels: '2016: 2 wolves', 'about 1,300 moose'. Counter races up to 'moose per wolf: 650' in white. The grey wolf line sits almost flat on the bottom of its panel from 2016 to 2018.
scenes.narration: Now jump to twenty sixteen. Scientists counted only two wolves on the whole island. They estimated one thousand three hundred moose. The counter shoots way up.

scenes.tts: With so much food, you might expect more wolves. That did not happen. The last wolves were close relatives. Mating between close relatives is called inbreeding.
scenes.visual: Two grey wolf icons stand beside a simple family tree diagram (schematic) whose branches loop back so the parents share the same grandparents. Label: 'inbreeding: mating between close relatives'.
scenes.narration: With so much food, you might expect more wolves. That did not happen. The last wolves were close relatives. Mating between close relatives is called inbreeding.

scenes.tts: The wolves carried harmful inherited traits, which added to their health problems. So a shortage of moose was not what held these wolves back.
scenes.visual: Small warning icons appear on the two wolf icons, labelled 'harmful inherited traits'. A pile of brown moose icons behind them is labelled 'plenty of food'. Text: 'food was not the limit here'.
scenes.narration: The wolves carried harmful inherited traits, which added to their health problems. So a shortage of moose was not what held these wolves back.

scenes.tts: Then people stepped in. In twenty eighteen and twenty nineteen, the Park Service brought nineteen new wolves to the island.
scenes.visual: Cartoon (schematic) of crates being opened on the island shore; grey wolf icons step out. On-screen label: '2018 and 2019: 19 new wolves brought in'. The graph's grey line begins to rise after 2018; the drawing stops at 2019.
scenes.narration: Then people stepped in. In twenty eighteen and twenty nineteen, the Park Service brought nineteen new wolves to the island.

scenes.tts: So food matters. Few moose for each wolf can mean fewer wolves. But weather, ticks, disease, inbreeding and people moving wolves also change the counts. Food is one limit on wolves, not the only one.
scenes.visual: The full graph shrinks to the left; on the right a list builds with icons: 'food availability (moose per wolf is only a rough clue)', 'weather', 'ticks', 'disease', 'inbreeding', 'people moving wolves'. The last sentence appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: So food matters. Few moose for each wolf can mean fewer wolves. But weather, ticks, disease, inbreeding and people moving wolves also change the counts. Food is one limit on wolves, not the only one.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex beside a small grey wolf and a brown moose. Line: 'Food is one limit on wolves, not the only one.'
